\chapter{Selling, Serving, Spending, Growing}
\label{ch:vender-y-servir}
\hlchaptermodality{386}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say vender, servir, gastar and crecer, and name four everyday actions.}

Complete ES-C386-crecer: name four everyday actions, and say one thing that grows.

\section[vender]{vender — two words squeezed into one}

\label{lesson:ES-C386-vender}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to mix}, then \emph{to hang}. (\emph{Mezclar}; \emph{colgar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la tienda — where selling happens.
  \item el precio — what it happens at.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ven-DER}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{v} is the same sound as \emph{b}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{vender} — \textquotedblleft{}to sell.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{vendere} looks like one word. It is two, worn down until the seam stopped showing.

The first half is \textbf{venum}, which meant \emph{for sale}. The second half is \textbf{dare}, to give. \emph{Venum dare} — to give something for sale. Say it quickly enough, for long enough, and it collapses into \emph{vendere}.

That is not a guess, and the proof is sitting in the verb's own other forms. Latin's past of \emph{dare} was \textbf{dedi}, and the past of \emph{vendere} is \textbf{vendidi} — with \emph{dedi} still visible inside it, unabsorbed. The same happens in \textbf{venditum}, which carries \emph{datum}. The compound wore down at the seam but the old forms did not.

There is a second clue, in the sound. The \emph{e} in \emph{vendere} is long, which is not what Latin normally does before \emph{-nd-}. Two words pressed together explain the oddity; nothing else does.

So the Latin for selling has a \textbf{giving} inside it. Spanish still keeps that second half on its own: \emph{dar}, to give, is the same verb, standing separately in the language beside the compound it was folded into.

English took the family from the outside. A \textbf{vendor} vends; a \textbf{vending} machine sells without a person. And the first half surfaces in \textbf{venal} — said of an official, a vote, a witness who can be \emph{bought}. That is \emph{venum} almost untouched: for sale.

One to refuse: a \textbf{vendetta} is not in this family. It comes from Latin \emph{vindicta}, revenge, and only looks the part.

It is a good habit to build. A Latin word that seems oddly short for its meaning is often two words that stopped being two — and the old past tenses are where you go looking for the seam.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{vender}. And you can take a Latin verb apart at a seam.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vender}
  \item \emph{vender la casa}
  \item \emph{el precio}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two words are inside \emph{vendere}? (\emph{Venum}, for sale; \emph{dare}, to give.) What does calling someone \emph{venal} say about them? (That they can be bought.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[servir]{servir — dessert is named for the clearing}

\label{lesson:ES-C386-servir}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to hang}, then \emph{to sell}. (\emph{Colgar}; \emph{vender}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la sopa — something you serve.
  \item el plato — what you serve it on.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ser-VIR}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{v} is the same sound as \emph{b}, and both \emph{r} sounds are single taps. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{servir} — \textquotedblleft{}to serve.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{servire} was built on \textbf{servus}, a slave. To serve, at the bottom of the word, was to \emph{be} one. Everything polite about the modern verb is a coat of paint over that.

Where \emph{servus} itself came from is not agreed. One reading takes it back to an older word for a \emph{guardian}, soured into \textquotedblleft{}slave\textquotedblright{} somewhere in early Italy; another suspects Rome borrowed it from the Etruscans. The dictionaries that report both end by saying the matter is uncertain, so the trail stops at the slave.

The word to chase is \textbf{dessert}, because almost nobody reads it.

French \textbf{desservir} means to \emph{un}-serve: to clear the table, to take away what was served. The noun made from it, \emph{dessert}, named the part of the meal that came after the clearing. So the sweet course is not named for being sweet. It is named for the moment the plates went out.

Next, a pair. \textbf{Servant} and \textbf{sergeant} are the same Latin word, arriving in English twice by two roads — Medieval Latin \emph{servientem}, one who is serving. In the sixteenth century English writers still used the two more or less interchangeably. One of them then walked into the army and the other stayed in the house.

And \textbf{deserve} is \emph{de-} plus \emph{servire}: to serve thoroughly, to serve well. To deserve something was to have earned it by service. The word remembers a transaction that English speakers no longer hear. When somebody gets their \textbf{deserts}, that word is \emph{deserve} wearing a noun's coat — nothing to do with the sandy kind.

One thing not to over-read. Spanish does not call the sweet course a \emph{dessert}. It says \textbf{postre}, from a Latin word meaning \emph{what comes after}. The clearing of the table is the French picture, not the Spanish one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{servir}. And you can say what \emph{dessert} is really named after.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{servir}
  \item \emph{servir la sopa}
  \item \emph{el plato}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{dessert} name — the food or the clearing? (The clearing: to un-serve the table.) Which English word is \emph{servant} arriving a second time? (\emph{Sergeant}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gastar]{gastar — spending, and laying waste}

\label{lesson:ES-C386-gastar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to sell}, then \emph{to serve}. (\emph{Vender}; \emph{servir}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el dinero — what you spend.
  \item la cuenta — what tells you how much.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gas-TAR}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{g} before \emph{a} is hard, as in \emph{gato}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{gastar} — \textquotedblleft{}to spend.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{vastare} meant to lay waste, to ruin, to empty a country out. Spanish took that verb and pointed it at a purse. Spending money is laying it waste.

The clean English relative is \textbf{devastate} — \emph{de-} plus \emph{vastare}, to lay waste completely. Nothing has been bent on the way; it is the Latin verb with a prefix.

English \textbf{waste} is the interesting one, because it did not arrive clean.

Old North French had \emph{waster}, and \emph{waster} is Latin \emph{vastare} after a West Germanic word of similar sound and meaning had leaned on it. That leaning left a mark you can still hear: English opens the word with \textbf{w}, while the Romance side opens it with \textbf{g} — \emph{gastar}. The \emph{w} is the Germanic fingerprint on a Latin word, and Spanish sits on the other side of the same split.

The Academy's dictionary gives \emph{gastar} one line and mentions none of this. It is not wrong; it is short. An entry can be right about the ancestor and silent about what happened on the road.

One thing to leave alone. It is tempting to add \textbf{vast} to the pile. Latin \emph{vastus} meant both \emph{huge} and \emph{empty, desolate} — and those two senses probably belonged to two different words that fell together early in Latin. So \emph{vast} may not be the same word as \emph{vastare} at all, and the honest move is not to claim it.

And a trap worth naming: \textbf{gastric}, \textbf{gastronomy} and the rest are Greek \emph{gaster}, a belly. They have nothing to do with \emph{gastar}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{gastar}. And you can read a \emph{w} as a fingerprint.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gastar}
  \item \emph{gastar el dinero}
  \item \emph{la cuenta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the \emph{w} in \emph{waste} come from, when the Romance side has a \emph{g}? (A West Germanic word that leaned on the Latin one.) Is \emph{gastronomy} a relative? (No — Greek for belly.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[crecer]{crecer — the moon caught in the act}

\label{lesson:ES-C386-crecer}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to serve}, then \emph{to spend}. (\emph{Servir}; \emph{gastar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el árbol — something that grows.
  \item el niño — something else that grows.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cre-CER}, two beats with the weight on the second. The first \emph{c} is a hard \emph{k}; the second, before \emph{e}, is soft. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{crecer} — \textquotedblleft{}to grow.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{crescere}, to grow. Said like that it is a circle, so here are the two places the verb went and stopped looking like itself.

The first is over your head. Latin called the waxing moon \textbf{luna crescens} — the \emph{growing} moon. English kept the second half and dropped the moon: \textbf{crescent}. The shape is not named for being a curve. It is named for a \emph{direction} — a moon on its way up. A moon on its way down is the same curve and is not a crescent.

Musicians borrowed the Italian form of the same word for the same idea: \textbf{crescendo}, growing, and what grows is the sound.

The second is stranger. A \textbf{recruit} is a soldier newly joined. The word came through French \emph{recrue}, from a verb meaning \emph{to grow again} — \emph{re-} on the front of the same \emph{crescere}. An army that has lost people and taken on new ones has, in the picture the word paints, \textbf{grown back}. A recruit is a fresh growth. A ship's \textbf{crew} started in the same place: an increase in hands.

And one that sits closer to home. Spanish \emph{crear}, to create, is the older partner of this verb: Latin \emph{creare} is the \emph{causing} form, to \textbf{make} grow, while \emph{crescere} is the plain one, to grow. Creating and growing were one idea with two settings.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{crecer}. And you know why only one of the two curved moons is a crescent.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{crecer}
  \item \emph{el árbol}
  \item \emph{gastar y crecer}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a crescent moon, in Latin? (\emph{Luna crescens} — the growing moon.) What is a recruit, taken word for word? (A fresh growth.)
\end{tcolorbox}
